What is BERTScore or other embedding-based metrics, and can they be helpful in evaluating the similarity between a generated answer and a reference answer or source text? BERTScore is an embedding-based metric used to evaluate the similarity between texts by leveraging contextual embeddings from models like BERT. Unlike traditional metrics such as BLEU or ROUGE, which rely on exact word matches or n-gram overlaps, BERTScore compares texts by measuring the semantic similarity of their token or sentence embeddings. Other embedding-based metrics include MoverScore, which uses optimal transport to align embeddings, and Sentence-BERT, which computes sentence-level similarities. Embedding-based metrics work by converting text into high-dimensional vectors using pre-trained language models. For example, BERTScore computes token-level embeddings for both the generated and reference texts, then calculates precision, recall, and F1 scores based on cosine similarity between these embeddings. If a generated answer uses synonyms or rephrases concepts (e.g., “canine” instead of “dog”), BERTScore can recognize the semantic equivalence even if surface-level words differ. Similarly, Sentence-BERT generates a single embedding per sentence, enabling efficient comparison of entire sentences or paragraphs. Embedding-based metrics are helpful for evaluating answer similarity but have trade-offs. However, these metrics require computational resources to generate embeddings and may not always correlate perfectly with human evaluation. Developers should consider combining embedding-based metrics with traditional methods and human evaluation for a balanced assessment, especially in critical applications like fact-checking or legal document analysis. results.title: Understanding Cosine Similarity and Word Embeddings | by Spencer Porter | Medium
results.content: # Understanding Cosine Similarity and Word Embeddings. ## What is Cosine Similarity? Cosine Similarity measures the cosine of the angle between two vectors. Words that are semantically similar will have vectors pointing in similar directions, resulting in a higher Cosine Similarity. ## Evaluating LLMs Using Cosine Similarity. Here, Cosine Similarity can be invaluable. You could evaluate its performance by comparing the Cosine Similarity between the generated description and a human-written description for the same product. A high Cosine Similarity would indicate that the model has generated a description closely aligned with human expectations. # Sample human-written descriptionhuman_description = "This laptop has a sleek design, high-resolution display, and long battery life."# Sample LLM-generated descriptionllm_description = "Featuring a slim design, this laptop offers a vibrant screen and extended battery duration."# Generate embeddings for both descriptionsembeddings_human = openai_session.generate_embeddings(human_description)embeddings_llm = openai_session.generate_embeddings(llm_description)# Compute Cosine Similaritysimilarity_score = cosine_similarity(embeddings_human, embeddings_llm)print(f"Cosine Similarity between human-written and LLM-generated descriptions: {similarity_score}"). Understanding the mechanics of word embeddings and the intuitive nature of Cosine Similarity can significantly enhance your ability to develop and evaluate text-based machine learning models.

results.title: Why I Chose Cosine Similarity & GPT Evaluation Over BLEU, ROUGE, and METEOR for LLM Response Evaluation | by Suhas Pawar | Towards AI
results.content: # **Why I Chose Cosine Similarity & GPT Evaluation Over BLEU, ROUGE, and METEOR** for LLM Response Evaluation. A few days back, I was knee-deep in evaluating AI-generated responses for one of my project in Gen AI. I found that no existing market solution was great at evaluating AI responses accurately. ✅ **Cosine Similarity (SBERT)** — To measure the semantic closeness of responses. In this blog, I’ll explain why traditional metrics fall short and why **Cosine Similarity & GPT Evaluation** provide a better way to measure AI-generated responses. * **Issue for AI evaluation**: Penalizes paraphrased but correct responses. 💡 ***AI Response*:** *“The meeting is at 10 AM tomorrow.”* ✅ *(Correct, but paraphrased)*. *🔻* ***BLEU Score****:* Low ❌ (Different word order, penalized). * **Issue for AI evaluation**: Can give **high scores to irrelevant but long responses**. **💡 *AI Response*:** *“Regulations mandate user consent for personal data collection.”* ✅ *(Correct meaning, different words)*. 💡 ***AI Response*:** *“Paris is the capital of France.”* ✅ *(Correct meaning, different order)*. *🔻* ***METEOR Score****:* Penalized ❌ (Different word order, even though meaning is the same). ## **🚀 Why I Chose Cosine Similarity + GPT Evaluation**. ✅ **Cosine Similarity (SBERT)** — Measures **semantic closeness** instead of word matching. ✅ **GPT-based Evaluation** — Understands **context, nuance, and factual accuracy**. Cosine Similarity Captures Meaning, Not Just Words**. Instead of relying on **exact word matches**, Cosine Similarity (using SBERT embeddings) **compares the actual meaning** of sentences. 💡 ***AI Response:*** *“The company provides 20 days of paid vacation per year.”* ✅ *(Same meaning, different words)*. ✔ **Cosine Similarity Score**: **~0.95 (High, meaning is the same)**. 💡 ***AI Response 1*:** *“Microsoft was established in 1975 by Bill Gates and Paul Allen.”* ✅ *(Correct, different wording)*. 💡 ***AI Response 2*:** *“Microsoft was founded in 1985 by Steve Jobs.”* ❌ *(Incorrect fact)*. **💡 Final Verdict: Why My Approach is Better for AI Evaluations**. * GPT compares both responses based on **meaning, accuracy, and context**. **Cosine Similarity Score + GPT Confidence Score**. 👉 That’s why I built a **Streamlit app** using Cosine Similarity + GPT Evaluation! ### **🔗** **Related Blog:** Streamlit-Powered **Automated Response Evaluation: Leverage AI to Score & Visualize Model Performance**.

results.title: Understanding Statistical Measures of Text Similarity
results.content: # Understanding Statistical Measures of Text Similarity. One of the critical methodologies to understand when implementing text data is text similarity. The ability to measure text similarity has become essential to understanding the relationship between text content. In this article, we will learn several statistical measurements for text similarity. ## Text Similarity Measurement. When we speak of text similarity, we are referring to the measurement of the quantified resemblance degree between two texts. 1. The **lexical similarity** involves comparing texts based on surface-level features such as word matching or n-grams overalls. 2. **Semantic similarity** focuses more on the meaning behind the text, even with different words in the texts. Using statistical methods, we can quantify the text similarity and provide insight into the text relationship. Jaccard similarity measures the proportion of the shared elements between two texts compared to the total unique words in both texts. The Jaccard similarity measurement works best when the presence of words is much more important than the frequency. A smaller measurement or distance means the two texts are more similar. Levenshtein distance is a measurement of text similarity that calculates the transformation number of operations required to transform one string into another. And that’s the basic of statistical text similarity measurements. * Optimizing the Levenshtein Distance for Measuring Text Similarity. 1. Hi Brian…Semantic similarity metrics are crucial for comparing text-based data, especially in NLP tasks like clustering, search, recommendation systems, and question-answering. 1. \*\*Jaccard Similarity\*\* – Measures overlap between two sets of words or characters. 2. \*\*Cosine Similarity\*\* – Uses TF-IDF or word frequency vectors to compute the cosine of the angle between two document vectors. 7. \*\*Cosine Similarity (on Word Embeddings)\*\* – Computes the cosine angle between word vectors (works well for high-dimensional spaces). 8. \*\*BERTScore\*\* – Uses contextual embeddings from BERT to compute similarity. \*\*SIF (Smooth Inverse Frequency) Embeddings\*\* – Improves word vector similarity by reducing common word effects. – \*\*Short text similarity\*\* → Cosine similarity on TF-IDF, Jaccard Similarity. – \*\*Sentence similarity\*\* → SBERT, USE, Cosine Similarity on embeddings. – \*\*Document similarity\*\* → Word Mover’s Distance, BERTScore. – \*\*Low-resource tasks\*\* → Edit distance, Jaccard, or Dice Similarity.
